title: What can be done with Shaders? (2D)
author: LiquidZebra
selftext:
I saw a post here of a guy who made a full 3D game with shaders for textures. 

What can be done for a 2D game with a semi-realistic art style, no pixel art, isometric sprite projection, uniform lighting, no glow of flashy effects:

Can I code a helmet as a texture that fits a head?

Can I code a face? (Wrote a tool that modifies existing art,  but would like to know more techniques , names or repos)

Weapons, armor, visible damage?

Breathing, blinking or other animations?

Holograms (I rigged a 2D face into a point cloud, it kinda works, but I would like something more interesting )

I feel like I’m looking at a very promising area, because things just appear if I know what to ask for. But the second time I talked with Gaussian splats - they just don’t look good enough.

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body: Shaders are not effective for many things you describe. For sure, you can create a face or a helmet with code, but that starts to eat compute and make it heavy. GPUs were originally pretty much just made to render textures very efficiently, and that's still a good rule to follow. But for things like damage or other effects they are for sure excellent, and many times the best choice. It might be a good idea to take a look at some shader/VFX tutorials or such, just to get some frame of reference what generally is done and what's the split in those effects between textures and shaders.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
You are asking 2 questions: Whether you can make certain things for a 2D game procedurally and what you can do with shaders.

There are a lot of posts here about procedural generation of 2D artwork. The trick is usually to render a model in 3D from different angles. Why you then want to make a 2D game at all is questionable...

Shaders can definitely be used for frame post processing, such as retro effects or HDR tone mapping, bloom, etc.

Shaders can be used for procedural overlay textures, such as grime, damage, dirt, wear, burn marks, etc.

You can use shaders for pretty much anything that can be computed faster on a GPU than on a CPU. Just make sure to optimise properly and maybe occlusion cull whatever has expensive fragment shaders to reduce overdraw and unnecessary computation.

You can precompute procedural textures and meshes on a GPU and then read them as stayic textures or vertex buffers in regular frame rendering. And instead of precomputing a full RGB or HDR float texture, you can precompute just one expensive function of yiur procedural texture and still do the rest in a real-time shader.

You can even use compute shaders for non-graphical things as collision detection and physics. Just keep in mind that if you ever want to run your game on a dedicated server, there will be no GPU to run it. You can still use this in peer-to-peer multiplayer games. Whether you should is a different question. Profile your code first and fint out what actually takes time on the CPU, and if something takes way below a millisecond, probably keep it on the CPU...
